### case_derived_1091: Daily Wager Termination — Labour Law *(Two-track · Labour)*

**Junior Advocate:** Our client worked as a daily-wage loader for a state-owned goods corporation for eight years. He was simply told one day not to report for work. He has no appointment letter, no formal termination. What legal arguments are available?

*Decision dimension targeted: Regularization vs. reinstatement vs. compensation*
*Why this question wins: The available remedies differ — regularization is available under certain schemes, reinstatement for retrenchment without compliance, or compensation; identifying the viable claim avoids building the wrong case.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "File a writ immediately for reinstatement.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Without establishing the legal relationship and the applicable remedy, the writ is premature and may be rejected for non-exhaustion of labour remedies.*

**Senior Advocate:** For a daily-wage workman in continuous employment for eight years, the primary legal avenue is the Industrial Disputes Act. The cessation of work without notice or retrenchment compensation under Section 25-F is an illegal retrenchment — the workman is entitled to one month's notice or pay in lieu and retrenchment compensation at fifteen days' wages per year of service. If the retrenchment was not preceded by this compliance, it is void and the workman is entitled to reinstatement with back wages. We first establish whether the Industrial Disputes Act applies — which it does for a "workman" as defined — and then file a reference or a complaint before the Labour Court.

**Junior Advocate:** The corporation will argue the client was not a "workman" but an independent daily-wage contractor with no employment relationship. How do we establish the employment relationship without an appointment letter?

*Decision dimension targeted: Proof of employment relationship from conduct and circumstances*
*Why this question wins: The absence of formal documentation is common in daily-wage arrangements; courts use a functional test for employment relationship.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Concede the issue of employment relationship and focus on compensation."*
*Why bad alternative loses: Without proving employment, no remedy under the ID Act is available; the employment relationship must be established.*

**Senior Advocate:** Employment is established by the functional control test: who directed the work, who controlled the timing and method, who supplied materials or tools, and who had the power to terminate. Daily-wage loaders directed by a supervisor at the corporation's premises, loading and unloading the corporation's goods, under the corporation's daily supervision, are employees in substance regardless of the label. We present wage slips if available, co-worker affidavits, ESI or PF records if deductions were made, and any identity card or gate pass issued by the corporation. Any one of these is powerful corroboration of the employment relationship.

**Junior Advocate:** The Labour Court decides in our favour but awards only three months' wages as "lump sum compensation" instead of reinstatement. Is this adequate?

*Decision dimension targeted: Adequacy of lump-sum compensation as a substitute for reinstatement*
*Why this question wins: The ID Act default is reinstatement with back wages; substituting it with lump sum requires justification and the right quantum.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Accept the lump-sum and advise the client to move on.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Three months' wages after eight years of service and illegal retrenchment is grossly inadequate; an appeal against the quantum is clearly available.*

**Senior Advocate:** Reinstatement is the primary remedy for illegal retrenchment under the ID Act. Lump-sum compensation may be substituted if the workman's reinstatement is shown to be impractical — typically because the workman was one of many, the post no longer exists, or the employer-employee relationship has irretrievably broken down. Three months' wages for eight years of service is not adequate lump-sum compensation by any standard; the Supreme Court's formula pegs it at reasonable proximity to what the workman would have earned until normal retirement or a meaningful severance. We appeal the quantum to the High Court.

---

### case_derived_1092: Pension Rule Fairness — Double Cut Challenge *(Two-track · Service Law)*

**Junior Advocate:** Our client received a promotion-based pay revision five years before retirement. The pension rules treat the last ten years' average emoluments for computing pension, but because the promotion happened just before the five-year mark, the higher salary for only the last five years drags down the average. Can we challenge the formula as unfair?

*Decision dimension targeted: Challenge to pension computation formula vs. benefit of doubt interpretation*
*Why this question wins: A formula that systematically disadvantages employees who received promotions just before the cutoff may be challenged as arbitrary — but only if a better statutory interpretation is available, not merely because the result is uncomfortable.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Argue the pension should be computed on the last pay drawn.*
*Why bad alternative loses: The rule specifying the averaging period is express; a simple argument for last-pay-drawn ignores the statutory text.*

**Senior Advocate:** The first question is whether the applicable pension rules actually say "last ten years' average" or whether they have been amended. Many central government pension rules have moved to "last pay drawn" or "average of last ten months" — we must read the exact applicable rule for our client's service. If the rule does say ten years' average, the constitutional challenge is that a rule which computes benefits by averaging over a period that straddles a promotion creates an arbitrary outcome — an employee promoted just before the halfway point is systematically penalised compared to one promoted ten years before retirement. Courts have struck down anomalous pension computation rules as arbitrary under Article 14.

**Junior Advocate:** The department says the rules are uniform — the same formula applies to everyone — and uniformity means there is no arbitrariness. How do we counter this?

*Decision dimension targeted: Uniformity vs. rationality — Article 14 analysis*
*Why this question wins: Article 14's guarantee of equality requires that classifications be rational, not merely uniform; a uniformly applied irrational formula is still arbitrary.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Accept that uniformity defeats the constitutional challenge.*
*Why bad alternative loses: The Article 14 guarantee of reasonableness is independent of uniformity.*

**Senior Advocate:** Uniformity is necessary but not sufficient for constitutional validity. The question under Article 14 is whether the classification — grouping employees by averaging period in a way that creates a systematic disadvantage for those promoted in the middle period — has a rational nexus to the object of the pension rule. The object of pension is to secure a retirement benefit proportionate to the employee's career earnings and status. A formula that consistently under-compensates employees with mid-career promotions defeats that object. We argue the formula is unreasonable in its application to a defined sub-class and seek judicial correction through interpretation or, if necessary, declaration.

**Junior Advocate:** Is there a way to read the rule more favourably without attacking it as unconstitutional?

*Decision dimension targeted: Interpretive remedy before constitutional challenge*
*Why this question wins: Courts prefer saving statutes and rules through interpretation; offering an interpretation-based route alongside the constitutional challenge is good advocacy.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Lead only with the constitutional challenge.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Constitutional challenges take longer; an interpretation-based argument can produce the same result faster.*

**Senior Advocate:** We should argue that the rule, properly interpreted, permits computing pension on the "highest emoluments drawn for any continuous twelve-month period" during service — a reading some courts have adopted where the averaging language is ambiguous. Alternatively, we argue the rule should be read to pick the average during the period when the promoted salary was received, not blended with the pre-promotion period. This interpretive argument does not require us to attack the rule as unconstitutional — it asks the court to give the rule a reading that fulfils its purpose. We present the constitutional argument as an alternative if the interpretive one fails.

---

### case_derived_1093: High Court Writ for Stay of Income Tax Assessment *(Two-track · Income Tax)*

**Junior Advocate:** Our client received a reassessment order under Section 148 of the Income Tax Act for an assessment year that is already nine years old. He believes the reassessment is barred by limitation. Can we go directly to the High Court?

*Decision dimension targeted: Writ maintainability vs. appellate statutory remedy*
*Why this question wins: A pure limitation issue — where the assessment is void on the face of the record — is one of the recognised exceptions to the rule that statutory remedies must be exhausted first.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "File a standard appeal before the CIT(A) and then ITAT.*
*Why bad alternative loses: While the appellate route is available, a time-bar argument is a jurisdictional point that can be raised before the High Court directly, saving years of litigation.*

**Senior Advocate:** The general rule is that tax matters should be resolved through the CIT(A)–ITAT–High Court appellate ladder. However, the Supreme Court has held that where an assessment order is wholly without jurisdiction — including cases where it is palpably barred by limitation — the High Court can entertain a writ petition under Article 226 without requiring exhaustion of the statutory remedy. A reassessment beyond the maximum limitation period prescribed by Section 149 is a nullity, not merely an irregularity. We argue that the writ is maintainable on this basis and accompany it with a calculation showing the limitation breach on the face of the record.

**Junior Advocate:** The Income Tax department will argue that the limitation question involves facts — such as when information was received by the AO and whether foreign asset connection existed — and therefore the High Court should not entertain a writ but leave it to the statutory process. How do we respond?

*Decision dimension targeted: Pure law question vs. fact-dependent limitation issue*
*Why this question wins: If the limitation bar is apparent from the record without needing factual inquiry, the writ is maintainable; if facts are genuinely disputed, the High Court may decline.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Concede factual disputes exist and move only in the CIT(A).*
*Why bad alternative loses: If the limitation breach is apparent from the plain record, there is no reason to concede factual disputes where none exist.*

**Senior Advocate:** We examine the reassessment notice carefully. Section 149 prescribes the limitation period — for most cases it is six years; for certain asset-based or undisclosed foreign asset cases it extends. If the department claims to invoke the extended period, it must show in the notice itself that the case falls within that category. If the notice does not identify any basis for the extended limitation and the relevant assessment year is beyond the six-year period, the limitation bar is facially apparent and no fact-finding is required. We make this argument explicitly — "the limitation defect appears on the face of the record, there are no disputed facts" — to take the High Court's concern about fact-finding off the table.

**Junior Advocate:** Even if the writ is maintainable, should we also file a protective appeal before the CIT(A) simultaneously?

*Decision dimension targeted: Protective appeal as a precautionary measure*
*Why this question wins: If the High Court declines to entertain the writ and the appeal limitation period expires, the client is left without remedy; a protective appeal preserves the statutory route.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Rely entirely on the writ and skip the appeal.*
*Why bad alternative loses: If the High Court declines the writ on the ground that statutory remedies must be exhausted, and the appeal is time-barred by then, the client has no remedy.*

**Senior Advocate:** Always file the CIT(A) appeal within time as a protective measure, even when you believe the writ will succeed. The writ and the appeal can run concurrently. You inform the High Court of the protective appeal so there is no issue of parallel proceedings. If the High Court entertains the writ and grants relief, the appeal becomes infructuous. If the High Court declines the writ, the appeal is already alive and the client's position is preserved. In high-stakes matters, never leave the client without a fallback.

---

### case_derived_1094: Termination After Appointment Legality Review *(Two-track · Service Law)*

**Junior Advocate:** A state government reviewed all appointments made over the previous five years and found that our client was appointed without proper procedure. They have terminated her. She has worked for four years. What is the legal position?

*Decision dimension targeted: Termination vs. regularization after appointment legality review*
*Why this question wins: The legal consequences of an irregular appointment depend on whether the employee was at fault, whether the post was genuine, and what period of service has elapsed.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Challenge the legality review itself.*
*Why bad alternative loses: While the review process can be challenged, attacking the core finding of procedural irregularity is difficult; the more effective argument focuses on remedy.*

**Senior Advocate:** An irregular appointment — one made without following prescribed procedures — does not automatically make the employee a wrongdoer, especially if she had no knowledge of the procedural irregularity and relied on the appointment letter issued by the government. The Supreme Court in multiple cases has held that a government servant cannot be visited with termination for the sin of the appointing authority. The correct approach is: regularize those who are eligible; for those who cannot be regularized, provide notice, an opportunity to apply through proper channels, and appropriate compensation. Summary termination after four years without a show-cause is procedurally improper.

**Junior Advocate:** The government says because the original appointment was void, there is no employment relationship and therefore no termination procedure is required. Is this argument legally sound?

*Decision dimension targeted: Void appointment vs. de facto employee status*
*Why this question wins: A legally void appointment still creates a de facto employment relationship; natural justice protections apply to de facto employees.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Accept the void appointment argument and move to compensation only.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Accepting void appointment concedes all substantive remedies; the de facto employee argument preserves reinstatement as a potential relief.*

**Senior Advocate:** The argument that a void appointment negates all employment rights has been expressly rejected by the Supreme Court. A de facto employee — one who has worked under an official appointment letter, received salary from the public exchequer, and performed government duties — cannot be dismissed without a show-cause notice, an opportunity to respond, and a reasoned order. The void character of the original appointment affects the question of whether permanent regularization is available, but it does not strip the de facto employee of basic procedural rights. The termination without show-cause is independently bad regardless of the appointment's validity.

**Junior Advocate:** The government is willing to "re-appoint" her through a proper process but warns that she must participate in the recruitment competition. Is this acceptable?

*Decision dimension targeted: Fresh recruitment as remedy vs. seamless continuity*
*Why this question wins: Fresh recruitment may be a legitimate part of the remedy but must be conducted fairly and with credit for established competence; the terms must be negotiated carefully.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Accept the fresh recruitment offer without conditions.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Accepting without conditions forfeits the argument for back-wages, continuous service credit, and seniority — all of which may be available.*

**Senior Advocate:** A regulated process is appropriate but the client should insist on: continuity of service from date of original appointment for seniority and pensionable service purposes; payment of arrears for the period between termination and re-appointment; and that the fresh recruitment process be fair and not used as a device to exclude her. We should seek these conditions through negotiation or through the writ petition. Courts have, in appropriate cases, directed that workers whose irregular appointments are set aside be given a fresh process in which their demonstrated work experience is given appropriate weight.

---

### case_derived_1095: Director — NI Act Prosecution *(Two-track · Cheque Bounce)*

**Junior Advocate:** Our client is a non-executive director of a company. The company issued a cheque that bounced. He has been personally arraigned in Section 138/141 NI Act proceedings. What is the specific legal protection available to him?

*Decision dimension targeted: Section 141 vicarious liability conditions for directors*
*Why this question wins: Section 141 NI Act creates vicarious liability only for specific categories of persons; non-executive directors who were not in charge of day-to-day conduct of business are excluded.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Argue the cheque was not issued by our client personally.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Section 141 is specifically about vicarious liability — the director does not have to sign the cheque personally; whether he is in charge of day-to-day business is the key test.*

**Senior Advocate:** Section 141 makes every person "in charge of, and responsible to, the company for the conduct of the business of the company" at the time the offence was committed liable. The Supreme Court has interpreted "in charge of" to mean effective control over the daily affairs of the company — not ceremonial or formal connection. A non-executive director who does not participate in day-to-day financial transactions, does not sign cheques, has no signatory authority over the account, and attends board meetings only for strategic governance is generally not "in charge" in this sense. We apply to quash the complaint against him under Section 482 CrPC.

**Junior Advocate:** The complainant's counsel will argue that our client appeared in the Annual Report as a director and that the company's website listed him as responsible for finance oversight. How do we rebut this?

*Decision dimension targeted: Formal designation vs. actual control*
*Why this question wins: The NI Act test is actual, effective charge — not designation; formal descriptions in public documents must be distinguished from operational control.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Challenge the website and Annual Report as inadmissible.*
*Why bad alternative loses: They are likely admissible; the better argument is that they describe formal designations, not operational control over the dishonoured transaction.*

**Senior Advocate:** We counter-produce the client's board attendance record showing limited, strategic-level participation; evidence that the finance function was operated by executive directors and the CFO; that the client had no signatory authority over the company's bank accounts; and any board resolutions delegating financial authority to specific executive persons. "Finance oversight" at the board level means setting financial policy — it does not mean controlling individual payment decisions. The Supreme Court has consistently held that a positive averment of operational charge is required in the complaint; a general designation is insufficient.

**Junior Advocate:** At what stage should we file the quashing petition — before the High Court or at the trial court stage?

*Decision dimension targeted: Timing of quashing vs. trial stage defence*
*Why this question wins: A director can either raise the defence at trial or seek early quashing; the right choice depends on whether the complaint is facially deficient on the Section 141 averment.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Await trial and raise the defence at the evidence stage.*
*Why bad alternative loses: If the complaint itself fails to make the necessary averment of day-to-day charge, quashing at the pre-trial stage is efficient and prevents years of litigation.*

**Senior Advocate:** If the complaint does not contain a specific averment that our client was in charge of the day-to-day conduct of the business of the company — which is a required ingredient as per Supreme Court rulings — we file a quashing petition before the High Court immediately under Section 482 CrPC. The absence of this specific averment is a legal defect on the face of the complaint that the High Court can address without any factual inquiry. If the complaint does contain the averment but we dispute it on facts, the defence is raised at trial through the evidence stage.

---

### case_derived_1096: Public Tender Challenge *(Two-track · Tender/Administrative)*

**Junior Advocate:** Our client submitted the lowest tender for a government road contract. The authority rejected his bid saying his experience certificates were "not in the required format" but accepted technically deficient bids from two other bidders. What is the legal argument?

*Decision dimension targeted: Discriminatory application of tender conditions*
*Why this question wins: Applying tender eligibility conditions selectively — strictly to one bidder and loosely to others — is arbitrary and amounts to favouritism.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Argue our client's experience certificates were adequate on merits.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Adequacy is a second-level argument; the discriminatory application argument is more direct and more damning.*

**Senior Advocate:** The principle of equal treatment in public procurement requires that eligibility conditions be applied uniformly. If the authority accepted deficiencies in other bidders' documents but rejected ours for a comparable or less significant deficiency, the rejection is discriminatory. We obtain through RTI the evaluation sheets showing how each bidder's documents were assessed. If the other bidders' documents had format or completeness issues that were excused while ours were not, this discrimination is the centrepiece of our writ petition.

**Junior Advocate:** The government argues that judicial review of technical evaluation in tenders is extremely limited and courts should not substitute their view for the expert authority's. How do we distinguish this principle from our case?

*Decision dimension targeted: Limited review of technical decisions vs. review for arbitrariness in eligibility assessment*
*Why this question wins: Courts do not evaluate which bid is technically superior but they do review discriminatory or unreasonable application of eligibility criteria.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Accept limited judicial review applies and shift to public interest grounds.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Accepting limited review as applying to eligibility discrimination cedes the strongest argument.*

**Senior Advocate:** The limited review principle applies to decisions about which technically qualified bidder's proposal is better — courts will not second-guess technical merit evaluations. However, the decision to qualify some bidders and disqualify others based on the same document deficiency is not a technical evaluation — it is an administrative decision to apply a standard selectively. Courts review such decisions for arbitrariness and discrimination without limiting themselves to deferential review. This is precisely the distinction drawn in Tata Cellular v. Union of India and subsequent judgments.

**Junior Advocate:** If we win the writ, what relief should we ask for — direct award to our client or fresh evaluation?

*Decision dimension targeted: Remedy in tender disputes*
*Why this question wins: Courts rarely award contracts directly; knowing what is obtainable guides the prayer.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Ask the court to award the contract to our client as the lowest bidder.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Courts do not normally order contract award; this prayer will be declined and may be seen as aggressive.*

**Senior Advocate:** The appropriate prayer is: first, quash the disqualification of our client; second, direct the authority to reconsider all bids by applying the eligibility criteria uniformly; third, direct that no final contract be signed during the pendency of the writ. If the contract has already been awarded, we seek quashing of the award and direction for fresh evaluation. In urgent infrastructure cases where the contract is already underway, courts may award damages equivalent to the lost profit margin instead of quashing the contract — so we should also include a damages prayer as an alternative to protect the client's interests.

---

### case_derived_1097: Retrenchment Relief Restoration *(Two-track · Labour)*

**Junior Advocate:** Our client was retrenched from a private firm and the Labour Court ordered reinstatement with back wages three years ago. The employer has not complied. What enforcement mechanisms are available?

*Decision dimension targeted: Enforcement of Labour Court award against non-compliant employer*
*Why this question wins: A Labour Court award is enforceable as a decree; identifying the specific enforcement mechanism moves the client from a paper victory to actual relief.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "File another complaint before the Labour Court.*
*Why bad alternative loses: The Labour Court has already issued the award; the issue is enforcement, not re-adjudication.*

**Senior Advocate:** A Labour Court award, once final, can be enforced as a decree of a civil court under Section 36 of the Industrial Disputes Act. The workman applies to the appropriate court — usually the civil court or the execution court — for execution of the award by attachment of the employer's property, bank accounts, and machinery. Simultaneously, the employer can be held in contempt if the award has been confirmed by the High Court. We must also ensure the award has not been challenged in a revision or writ — if a stay is operating, we must first vacate the stay.

**Junior Advocate:** The employer has challenged the award in the High Court and obtained a stay subject to payment of 25% of back wages. The employer has not paid even the 25%. What do we do?

*Decision dimension targeted: Conditional stay and non-compliance — contempt*
*Why this question wins: A conditional stay that is not complied with can be vacated and the employer held in contempt; this is often the most efficient path.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Apply for vacation of the stay on merits.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Vacation on merits takes time; non-compliance with the stay condition is a faster and stronger ground for vacation.*

**Senior Advocate:** We file an urgent application in the High Court writ stating that the stay was conditional on payment of 25% of back wages, that this condition has not been met, and seeking vacation of the stay on that ground. Courts routinely vacate conditional stays when conditions are not fulfilled. We simultaneously file an application for payment of the 25% arrears directly to the workman. If the employer still does not comply after the High Court direction, we file a contempt petition before the High Court for disobedience of the court's own order.

**Junior Advocate:** The employer says the company has no assets and no money to comply. Can we pierce the corporate veil to recover from the promoters personally?

*Decision dimension targeted: Lifting the corporate veil for labour award enforcement*
*Why this question wins: Courts have lifted the corporate veil to hold promoters personally liable for labour awards when asset-stripping is suspected.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Accept that the company's insolvency prevents recovery.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Accepting insolvency as a defence rewards deliberate asset-stripping and leaves the workman with nothing.*

**Senior Advocate:** If the employer company has deliberately stripped assets after the award to frustrate enforcement, we can apply to the court to lift the corporate veil and proceed against the promoters personally. We must show an absence of the formal separation of personality — evidence that the promoters used the company's assets as their own, intermingled personal and company funds, or transferred assets out of the company after the award. We also check whether the company is undergoing insolvency proceedings under the IBC, in which case our client is a workman with statutory priority in the resolution process.

---

### case_derived_1098: Motor Accident — Income and Dependency Calculation *(Two-track · Motor Accident)*

**Junior Advocate:** Our client's husband, a 38-year-old self-employed carpenter, died in a road accident. He had no income tax returns but his family estimates his monthly earnings at around Rs. 25,000. How does the Tribunal assess income for an informal sector worker?

*Decision dimension targeted: Proof and estimation of income for self-employed informally-employed deceased*
*Why this question wins: Absence of formal income documents does not bar compensation — courts have developed methods for estimating informal incomes, and knowing them drives the evidence strategy.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Claim only the minimum wage as income.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Minimum wage is a floor, not a ceiling, for informal workers; claiming only minimum wage dramatically undervalues the claim.*

**Senior Advocate:** For an informally employed person, income can be established through a combination of: testimony from the deceased's clients and co-workers; evidence of tools, equipment, and materials owned; bank deposit patterns; any invoices or receipts; and the prevailing market rate for skilled carpenters in that area. The Tribunal can also take judicial notice of the standard earnings in a trade if they are well-established. We present the family's evidence along with a market rate report from a local trade association or government skill development authority. The court must arrive at a reasonable estimate — it cannot deny compensation merely because formal proof is unavailable.

**Junior Advocate:** After estimating income, what multiplier should we use for a 38-year-old deceased?

*Decision dimension targeted: Correct multiplier under Sarla Verma / National Insurance formula*
*Why this question wins: The multiplier tables from these Supreme Court judgments are now binding and must be applied correctly; using the wrong multiplier is a common error with significant financial consequences.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Estimate the multiplier informally based on years until retirement.*
*Why bad alternative loses: The Supreme Court has standardised the multiplier table; informal estimation will be set aside on appeal.*

**Senior Advocate:** For a 38-year-old deceased, the National Insurance v. Pranay Sethi updated multiplier table specifies 16. We apply: estimated income minus one-third for personal expenses (standard deduction for a single bread-winner with dependants), then multiplied by 16. To this, we add the conventional heads: loss of estate, loss of consortium for the spouse, loss of love and affection for each minor child, and funeral expenses — all at the figures most recently updated by the Supreme Court. We ensure all these heads are specifically claimed so the Tribunal addresses each one.

**Junior Advocate:** The insurance company argues our client's husband was contributorily negligent because he was not wearing a helmet on a motorcycle. How does contributory negligence affect the award?

*Decision dimension targeted: Apportionment of contributory negligence in motor accidents*
*Why this question wins: Contributory negligence reduces the award proportionately; the quantum of reduction depends on the evidence and the court's assessment of fault.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Deny contributory negligence entirely to preserve the full claim.*
*Why bad alternative loses: If the evidence shows no helmet was worn, denial without counter-argument undermines credibility.*

**Senior Advocate:** We do not deny the factual allegation if it is supported by the post-mortem or police report. Instead, we argue: first, the nature of the accident and its primary cause — whether the colliding vehicle was the dominant cause — should determine the weight given to contributory negligence; second, courts typically do not reduce awards by more than 20–25% for helmet non-use unless the absence of the helmet was specifically the cause of death rather than the accident itself; third, in a fatal accident case, the widow and children should not be fully burdened by the deceased's omission. We argue for a nominal reduction or none at all if the injury was not a head injury.

### case_derived_1099: Bank Guarantee Encashment Dispute *(Two-track · Banking)*

**Junior Advocate:** Our client's company provided a bank guarantee in favour of a government entity under a construction contract. The government has now called upon the guarantee without giving any reason and our client says the invocation is fraudulent — no liability has crystallised. Can we restrain the bank from honouring the guarantee?

*Decision dimension targeted: Fraud exception to the autonomy principle of bank guarantees*
*Why this question wins: Bank guarantees are autonomous instruments; the only recognised exception to the bank's obligation to pay on demand is fraud, which must be established with a high threshold.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Argue the contract disputes are ongoing and therefore the guarantee cannot be encashed.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Pending contract disputes are not a defence to a bank guarantee — the autonomy principle is specifically designed to override them.*

**Senior Advocate:** The Supreme Court in U.P. State Sugar Corporation v. Sumac International and subsequent cases has upheld the "fraud exception" — a court will injunct payment of a bank guarantee only if the invocation is fraudulent on its face or would result in irretrievable injustice, and the fraud must be brought to the notice of the bank. Fraud means the beneficiary, by calling upon the guarantee, is making a fraudulent claim — for example, invoking a performance guarantee when no breach of performance has occurred and the invocation is being made solely to extract money with no underlying liability. Mere dispute about the liability does not constitute fraud.

**Junior Advocate:** Our client has written communications from the government entity acknowledging that the project was substantially completed and that the final payment was being processed. Would this constitute fraud if the guarantee is now called?

*Decision dimension targeted: Fraudulent invocation in the face of acknowledgment of performance*
*Why this question wins: An acknowledgment of performance followed by guarantee invocation — with no supervening event — is strong evidence of fraudulent purpose.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Argue the project was completed and therefore liability under the guarantee never crystallised.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Non-crystallisation of liability is the standard contract dispute argument; the fraud argument — based on the specific acknowledgment — is more compelling for an injunction.*

**Senior Advocate:** The written acknowledgment of substantial completion is critical. If the government entity acknowledged completion, received the benefit of the project, and is now calling the guarantee without identifying any fresh breach or outstanding obligation, the invocation is at least prima facie fraudulent. We file an urgent application before the High Court for an injunction restraining the bank from paying until the matter is decided. We exhibit the completion acknowledgment prominently. We also examine whether the guarantee was a performance guarantee or a payment guarantee — a performance guarantee may only be called if a defined performance failure has occurred.

**Junior Advocate:** The High Court may be reluctant to interfere with a bank guarantee given the autonomy principle. How do we overcome judicial reluctance?

*Decision dimension targeted: Meeting the high threshold for injunction against guarantee encashment*
*Why this question wins: The threshold is high but not impossible; understanding what elevates a case above the threshold allows us to present it correctly.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Argue balance of convenience without establishing the fraud threshold.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Balance of convenience is relevant only after the fraud threshold is crossed; jumping to convenience without establishing fraud will fail.*

**Senior Advocate:** We must establish: (a) clear and obvious fraud, not merely arguable fraud — the acknowledgment of completion makes this clearer than a typical dispute; (b) that the bank was aware of the fraud or that the circumstances made it so palpable that the bank had constructive knowledge; and (c) that irretrievable injustice will result if the guarantee is honoured — meaning the client company cannot recover the amount from the government entity even if it ultimately succeeds in arbitration. We also certify in the application that we are offering to keep the dispute amount in court, which substitutes for the guarantee and removes the urgency from the government's side while the fraud allegation is examined.

### case_derived_1100: Hostel Workers Regularization *(Two-track · Service Law)*

**Junior Advocate:** Our clients are forty hostel workers — cooks, cleaners, and maintenance staff — who have worked in a government university's hostels for twelve to fifteen years on daily wages. The university refuses to regularize them and is now threatening to outsource the work. What is their legal position?

*Decision dimension targeted: Uma Devi framework and outsourcing as a device*
*Why this question wins: The Uma Devi framework is the primary constraint on regularization; outsourcing as a tactic to avoid regularization obligations is a specific form of colourable exercise of power.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "File individual petitions for each worker.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Forty individual petitions will be expensive and slow; a representative or PIL filing in the High Court is more efficient and addresses the systemic issue.*

**Senior Advocate:** For workers with twelve or more years of service who joined before 2006 (the Uma Devi year), the first argument is the Uma Devi one-time exception for regularization. For those who joined after 2006, we look at whether the state or university has framed a regularization scheme since Uma Devi, and whether their cases fall within it. For all workers, the outsourcing threat is potentially a colourable exercise of power — if the university is outsourcing the identical functions to circumvent a court direction or anticipated regularization order, that is not a genuine outsourcing decision and can be challenged.

**Junior Advocate:** The university says the work is "non-core" and outsourcing is a legitimate management decision. How do we challenge this characterization?

*Decision dimension targeted: Core vs. non-core work in government institution context*
*Why this question wins: The "non-core" label is used to justify outsourcing; whether hostel upkeep is genuinely non-core in a residential university is factually contestable.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Accept the non-core characterization and focus only on regularization.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Accepting the characterization allows the outsourcing to proceed and undercuts the workers' employment claim.*

**Senior Advocate:** We argue that in a residential university, hostel operations — cooking, maintenance, sanitation — are not peripheral services but are essential to the university's residential character and affect students' welfare. We also argue that the timing of the outsourcing decision — coming after workers petitioned for regularization — is suspicious and should be explained by the university. Courts have set aside such "coincidental" outsourcing decisions when they appear to be responses to pending legal proceedings rather than genuine policy choices.

**Junior Advocate:** Even if regularization is not available, what other legal reliefs can these workers access?

*Decision dimension targeted: Alternative relief when regularization is unavailable*
*Why this question wins: Regularization is not the only remedy; minimum wage, gratuity, ESIC, and provident fund entitlements are independent of employment status.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Advise that without regularization, the workers have no remedy.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Multiple beneficial labour law entitlements exist independently of regular employment status.*

**Senior Advocate:** Even without regularization, the workers are entitled to: minimum wages under the Minimum Wages Act for the entire period of service; gratuity under the Payment of Gratuity Act after five years of continuous service; ESI and PF contributions if the establishment is covered; equal pay for equal work if their functions are identical to regularized employees; and fair process before any termination. We file for all these in parallel — before the Labour Commissioner, the EPFO, and the ESIC — creating a multi-front enforcement effort that gives the workers tangible immediate benefits while the regularization question is adjudicated.

### case_derived_1101: Export-Linked Tax Deduction *(Two-track · Income Tax)*

**Junior Advocate:** Our client is a software exporter who claimed a tax deduction under Section 10A/10B of the Income Tax Act for profits derived from export. The Assessing Officer has disallowed a portion of the deduction saying the profits were not "derived from export" but from domestic service. What is the legal argument?

*Decision dimension targeted: Nexus between profits and export activity for Section 10A/10B*
*Why this question wins: The deduction requires direct derivation from export; the dispute almost always turns on whether specific income has sufficient nexus to the export activity.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Argue the entire business is export-oriented and all profits qualify.*
*Why bad alternative loses: An overbroad claim that all profits qualify ignores the statutory text requiring derivation from the eligible unit; courts will not accept it.*

**Senior Advocate:** Section 10A/10B deduction is available for profits of an "undertaking" derived from export of articles or computer software. The statutory formula is: (export turnover / total turnover) × profits of the business. The AO may dispute the numerator — export turnover — by excluding certain receipts as domestic. We must examine whether the AO's exclusion is justified: the excluded receipts should be analysed against the definition of "export turnover" in the Explanation to Section 10A. Expenses incurred in India for services rendered outside India are not excluded from export turnover under the correct reading — a point frequently in dispute and largely resolved by the Supreme Court.

**Junior Advocate:** The AO has excluded from export turnover the amount received by our client for software support services provided to the foreign customer from India. Is this correct?

*Decision dimension targeted: Treatment of support services income in export turnover*
*Why this question wins: Support service income for foreign customers is a specific contested area; multiple court decisions have now clarified it.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Accept the exclusion for support services and claim deduction on the remainder.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Accepting the exclusion for support services concedes a significant amount without legal compulsion.*

**Senior Advocate:** The Supreme Court and multiple High Courts have held that services rendered from India to a foreign customer, even if they include support, maintenance, or teleservices, qualify as export of services for the purposes of Section 10A if the consideration is received in foreign exchange and the service is rendered by the eligible unit. The only income excluded from export turnover is expenses that are incurred outside India and are therefore deducted from export proceeds under the definition. Support services provided from India for a foreign client are exports of service — the AO's exclusion is legally incorrect.

**Junior Advocate:** What forum should we pursue — CIT(A), ITAT, or High Court — and at what stage does this become a "question of law"?

*Decision dimension targeted: Appellate path and when a question of law crystallises*
*Why this question wins: Tax matters follow a defined appellate path and High Court jurisdiction is limited to questions of law; understanding this determines strategy for each appellate stage.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Go directly to the High Court since the law is settled.*
*Why bad alternative loses: The High Court hears income tax appeals only from the ITAT, not directly from the AO or CIT(A); this procedural point cannot be skipped.*

**Senior Advocate:** We appeal to CIT(A) first, then to ITAT if unsuccessful. The ITAT decides both facts and law. Once the ITAT has decided, we can appeal to the High Court under Section 260A of the IT Act on a substantial question of law. The question "whether income from support services rendered from India to a foreign customer falls within export turnover for Section 10A deduction" is a well-established substantial question of law and qualifies for High Court reference. At each stage we also apply for stay of the demand as discussed in previous analyses.

### case_derived_1102: Criminal Bail in Corruption Case *(Two-track · Criminal)*

**Junior Advocate:** Our client, a mid-level public servant, has been arrested by the CBI under the Prevention of Corruption Act for allegedly accepting a bribe. He has been in custody for six months. What are the specific challenges in seeking bail in a PC Act case?

*Decision dimension targeted: Bail standards under Prevention of Corruption Act*
*Why this question wins: The PC Act does not contain a specific bail restriction like the PMLA or NDPS, but courts are generally strict; understanding the applicable standard determines how to structure the bail application.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Apply for bail under the general Section 439 CrPC provisions.*
*Why bad alternative loses: While Section 439 applies, bail in corruption cases must address the specific apprehensions courts have — tampering, public confidence, flight — and the standard application without this focus is routinely rejected.*

**Senior Advocate:** The Prevention of Corruption Act does not impose a statutory presumption against bail like the PMLA or the NDPS Act. The general bail principles under Section 439 CrPC apply — the court considers: nature and gravity of the offence, likelihood of flight, likelihood of tampering with witnesses, and the accused's antecedents. The challenge in PC Act cases is the court's perception that public servants who accept bribes should not be released quickly because it signals impunity. We need to address each apprehension specifically, not abstractly, with concrete undertakings and conditions.

**Junior Advocate:** The CBI will argue that our client has the capacity to influence witnesses and tamper with evidence because he is still a serving government officer. How do we neutralise this argument?

*Decision dimension targeted: Addressing tampering risk in bail arguments*
*Why this question wins: Tampering risk is the most persuasive ground for custody in corruption cases; addressing it with specific conditions is more effective than denying the risk abstractly.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Argue our client has no reason to tamper because he is innocent.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Innocence is the ultimate issue at trial, not a bail determination; courts at bail stage focus on risk management, not on resolving guilt.*

**Senior Advocate:** We offer specific, verifiable conditions that neutralise the tampering risk: our client undertakes not to contact or communicate with any person in his department or any witness; he undertakes to surrender his official phone and devices for periodic inspection; he is willing to reside at a specific address and report to the CBI station weekly; his passport is surrendered. We argue that continued custody when such conditions can address the risk is punitive, not protective. Six months in custody for a first-time offender in a non-violent corruption case — where the charge is a single transaction — is also relevant to the bail balance.

**Junior Advocate:** Six months have passed and no charge-sheet has been filed. Does this affect the bail analysis?

*Decision dimension targeted: Default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC*
*Why this question wins: If the charge-sheet has not been filed within sixty days for offences punishable with less than ten years, or ninety days for offences punishable with more than ten years, the accused is entitled to default bail as a matter of right.*
*Plausible bad alternative: "Continue arguing merits of regular bail without checking default bail entitlement.*
*Why bad alternative loses: Default bail under Section 167(2) is an indefeasible right if the period has expired; overlooking this is a serious error.*

**Senior Advocate:** This is the most critical question. Section 167(2) CrPC provides that if the charge-sheet is not filed within sixty or ninety days — depending on the maximum sentence — the Magistrate is bound to release the accused on bail if he applies for it. For offences under the PC Act punishable with up to seven years, the period is sixty days; for more serious charges, ninety days. We immediately verify whether any charge-sheet or supplementary charge-sheet was filed within the prescribed period. If not, we apply before the Magistrate for default bail under Section 167(2) — this right inures automatically and cannot be denied on the ground that the investigation is ongoing.
